before.title: 3.8L V6 Intake Manifold Gasket Coolant Leak
before.description: The 3.8L (3800) Series II V6 used in many Grand Prix models is prone to upper and lower intake manifold gasket failure, where the gasket degrades near the EGR/coolant passages and leaks coolant. Leaks can be external (visible coolant pooling, low coolant, overheating) or internal, allowing coolant to mix with engine oil and cause severe internal engine damage if driven. This is one of the most-reported problems for the platform and prompted multiple GM technical service bulletins.
before.solution: Replace the upper plastic intake manifold and both upper and lower intake manifold gaskets, ideally with upgraded aluminum-reinforced aftermarket gaskets (e.g., Fel-Pro). Flush the cooling system and change the oil immediately if coolant contamination is suspected. Inspect the EGR stovepipe area where the plastic manifold commonly melts.
symptoms: Coolant pooling or wet spots on engine

Check oil/coolant condition where warranted. Do not buy an upper manifold, gasket set, coolant or EGR-related part from this page; model year, engine/RPO, leak path, part number and VIN fitment must be established first.

before.title: 4T65-E Automatic Transmission Hard Shifting and Failure
before.description: The 4T65-E (and 4T65-E HD on the LS4 V8 GXP) automatic transmission commonly develops harsh/erratic shifting and eventual failure as mileage climbs. Causes include worn clutch packs, weak accumulator springs allowing slow shifts that trigger maximum line pressure, failing pressure control or shift solenoids, and the 4T65E-HD pan-magnet/line-pressure issue. Outright failure can leave the vehicle stranded with no warning.
before.solution: Diagnose with a scan tool for shift-quality codes; replace failing 1-2 shift solenoid or pressure control solenoid, service fluid and filter, and rebuild the unit (clutch packs/accumulators) when clutch material is worn. On the HD/GXP, inspect line pressure and the pan magnet.

The frozen accumulator, clutch-pack, solenoid and pan-magnet explanation collapses distinct unit/RPO, calibration, hydraulic, electrical and mechanical paths.
proposal.solution: Identify the transmission by VIN/RPO and capture codes, freeze-frame, commanded/actual gear, shift timing and temperature. Inspect fluid/debris, cooler flow and line pressure, then follow the code- and unit-specific tree before solenoid, valve-body, converter, clutch or unit replacement. Do not buy a solenoid, valve body, clutch kit, accumulator, magnet or transmission from this page; unit/RPO, failed path, calibration, part number and VIN fitment must be established first.

before.title: Engine Oil Leak onto Exhaust Manifold - Fire Risk (Recall 15V-201 / 08V-118)
before.description: GM recalled certain 1997-2004 Grand Prix vehicles because engine oil can drip from the front valve cover gasket onto the hot exhaust manifold, creating an engine-compartment fire risk that exists even when the vehicle is parked and unattended. The original remedies under recalls 08V-118 and 09V-116 did not fully resolve the hazard, so recall 15V-201 added an improved fix. Owners were advised to park outside until repaired.
before.solution: Have the recall performed at a GM/Pontiac dealer free of charge; the improved remedy replaces the front valve cover and gasket. Until repaired, park the vehicle outdoors away from structures. Verify recall completion by VIN at NHTSA.

before.title: HVAC Blower Motor Resistor Failure (Fan Stuck on High / Lost Speeds)
before.description: The blower motor resistor commonly fails, leaving the heater/AC fan working only on the highest setting or losing lower speeds (e.g., 1 and 2 dead while 3-5 work). Contributing factors include cowl water leaks dripping onto the resistor/connector and causing corrosion, and on 2004-2005 models a voltage spike from the wiper motor that can lock up the blower control module. The connector itself often melts and must be replaced.
before.solution: Replace the blower motor resistor and the wiring-harness connector together; replace the blower motor at the same time if worn to prevent repeat failure. For 2004-2005 control-module logic lockups, a GM TSB recommends installing a capacitor at the blower control module connector. Seal cowl leaks to prevent recurrence.
symptoms: Fan only works on highest speed

before.title: Ignition Switch May Slip Out of Run Position (Recall 14V400000)
before.description: As part of GM's massive 2014 ignition-switch recall (NHTSA campaign 14V400000, ~6.7 million vehicles), 2004-2008 Grand Prix were included because weight on the key ring, rough road conditions, or a jarring event can move the ignition switch out of the 'run' position, shutting off the engine. If the key leaves the run position, the airbags may not deploy in a crash, increasing injury risk.
before.solution: Complete the recall at a dealer free of charge; GM supplied replacement key rings and a key cover to reduce key-ring loading. As an interim measure, drivers were told to remove all extra items and fobs from the key ring, leaving only the ignition key.
symptoms: Loss of power steering and brakes when stalled

before.title: Key Sticks / Won't Turn or Come Out of Ignition
before.description: Owners frequently report the key becoming stuck in the ignition cylinder, unable to be removed or unable to turn to start, due to wear in the ignition lock cylinder and shift-interlock/Park-position issues. This is among the most-reported complaints for the seventh-generation cars (notably 2002), distinct from the 14V400000 switch recall. It can leave the vehicle unable to start or the key trapped.
before.solution: Verify the shifter is fully in Park and the brake/shift interlock is functioning; replace a worn ignition lock cylinder. Inspect the BTSI (brake-transmission shift interlock) solenoid and cylinder housing. Lubricating with the correct cylinder lubricant can help in mild cases.
symptoms: Key won't return / can't remove key

before.title: Supercharger Coupler Rattle (GTP / L67 Supercharged 3.8L)
before.description: On supercharged GTP models with the L67 (and the later L32 supercharged 3.8L), the Eaton M90 supercharger develops a noisy front coupler/isolator as the elastomer wears, producing a rattle or knock from the front of the blower. Owners report the rattle can return roughly 10,000 miles after a coupler replacement, and neglecting supercharger oil changes accelerates wear and reduces boost.
before.solution: Replace the supercharger coupler/isolator (remanufactured nose units are available); change the supercharger snout oil at the recommended interval, and inspect the belt, idlers, and vacuum lines. Address recurring rattle promptly to avoid further blower damage.
symptoms: Rattle or knock from front of supercharger
